newsitem.title: FRANCE: French unions sceptical on youth employment pact.
newsitem.headline: French unions sceptical on youth employment pact.

text.p: French ministers and employers sought to dispel trade union doubts on Tuesday that a pact to boost professional training for young people would significantly curb acute 25 percent youth unemployment.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe announced after a marathon meeting with industry, union and student leaders on Monday an agreement to ease the passage of students from school to work.

The accord provided for 400,000 youths to alternate study with periods of employment, backed by at least 750 million francs ($134 million) in government financial incentives to firms participating in the scheme.
The CNPF employers' federation agreed to supply by April a list of 100 to 150 big firms which would pledge to take in the equivalent of two percent of their total staff on such schemes.
Didier Pineau-Valenciennes, chairman of the Schneider group, said he felt employers were committed to the battle for jobs.
"Our contacts lead us to believe that all companies will participate," he said.

The government will also earmark one billion francs ($190 million) for local authorities to create jobs, help regional apprenticeship programmes and offer jobs in French firms abroad to 10,000 youths within the national service framework.
Education Minister Francois Bayrou said the accord marked a turning point. Although jobs were not created by decree, he felt business was making employment "the priority of priorities".
"1997 will be a test year for the young people," said Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot.
The Communist-led CGT union remained sceptical, saying the talks had again raised prospects of temporary employment and failed to tackle the issue of permanent jobs for school leavers.
CGT leader Louis Viannet said the youth jobs conference had "given birth to nothing, but then it wasn't pregnant".
The CGT stuck to its demands to make room for the young by cutting working hours and early retirement.

Juppe had insisted on practical solutions, and the daily Le Monde welcomed the accord as offering a range of provisions for the various categories of young job seekers. But it said the solutions offered fell short of the problem.
The issue of 600,000 young job-seekers will be crucial in next year's general election, and President Jacques Chirac has proclaimed a national "crusade" to help them find jobs.
France is among European countries worst hit by unemployment among people aged under 25 which stands at almost double the 12.7 percent national jobless rate, itself a record.

Despite plunging popularity and demands that the government give priority to employment, Chirac and Juppe are sticking to budget cuts and austerity policies designed to allow France to join the European single currency in 1999.
